analysis.one_liner: Requires the Agriculture Department to set and enforce limits on disease-causing pathogens in raw meat and poultry.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with one Republican among 10 cosponsors, was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the Agriculture Department to publish a list of the pathogens that cause the most foodborne illness, survey how contaminated raw meat and poultry actually are, and write pathogen-reduction standards set at what the best-performing processing plants already achieve. It would have required regular microbial testing at processing plants, and a plant that repeatedly failed a standard and did not fix the problem could no longer label its products 'inspected and passed.' It came after courts had ruled that the Department's existing legal authority to enforce pathogen limits was unclear, so the bill was written to remove that doubt.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who eats meat or poultry. Federal health authorities have long estimated that foodborne disease sickens millions of Americans each year, and raw meat and poultry are a significant source of the pathogens involved. The bill would have required standards based on what top-performing plants already achieve, regular testing to check compliance, and a real penalty for plants that keep failing, plus an independent scientific advisory committee to review food safety rules.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Agriculture Department to identify and publish a list of the pathogens most responsible for foodborne disease from meat and poultry, updated annually, and to survey current contamination levels at least every three years [S2][S3].

Requires pathogen-reduction standards set at the lowest contamination level reasonably achievable, using what the top quartile of plants already achieves as the benchmark, with final standards due within a year of each proposal [S2][S3].

Requires regular microbial testing at processing plants, and a plant that fails a standard and does not take corrective action can no longer label its products 'inspected and passed' — effectively barring those products from commerce [S2][S3].

Directs the Department to enforce Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Point (HACCP) and sanitation requirements at every inspected plant, and clarifies that its pathogen standards cannot be thrown out on the argument that the Department lacks authority to issue them [S2][S3].

Establishes a National Advisory Committee for Microbiology Criteria for Foods to give independent scientific advice on food safety standards, with conflict-of-interest rules barring members from voting on matters where they have a stake [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Meat and poultry processing plants, which would bear the cost of microbial testing, sanitation upgrades, and whatever process changes the standards require. Some of that cost would likely be passed to consumers in slightly higher meat prices.

drawbacks.text: Compliance and testing costs fall on processors, and some of those costs would be passed on to shoppers through meat and poultry prices [S3].

Denying the 'inspected and passed' label is a blunt enforcement tool: a plant that misses a standard loses the ability to sell its products into commerce even though it was never convicted of any violation, and the bill's deadlines (a pathogen list within 60 days, first standards within three years) were aggressive given the scientific work required [S3].

Benching standards off the top-performing quartile of plants assumes that performance is transferable across plants of different sizes and products; the bill left the detailed science largely to the Department to work out, which is where prior pathogen-rule fights had stalled [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside — fewer cases of foodborne illness, which causes hospitalizations and deaths each year and costs far more than the testing the bill required — substantially outweighed the compliance costs, and the bill tried to make those costs fair by benchmarking standards to what leading plants already achieve. Its main design weakness was the tight timetable and the reliance on label-denial as the enforcement lever rather than a graded penalty system. Still, it was a serious, workable attempt to fix a legal loophole that courts had opened in the government's food safety authority.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was read twice and sent to the Senate Agriculture Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the 108th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Tom Harkin introduced the bill on May 22, 2003, joined by six original cosponsors including Republican Arlen Specter [S3].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry [S5].
Ten senators cosponsored the bill in total — nine Democrats and one Republican [S4].
No further action appears in the record for the rest of the Congress: the bill never left committee and never received a floor vote [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Meat and poultry processing companies are better off: they never faced mandatory pathogen-reduction standards, regular microbial testing, or the threat of losing the 'inspected and passed' label that this bill would have imposed.

for.name: Sen. Tom Harkin
for.role: U.S. Senator from Iowa; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks; as a senior member of the Agriculture Committee he was its lead advocate.

for.name: Sen. Arlen Specter
for.role: U.S. Senator from Pennsylvania; original cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, the only Republican among the original six.

for.name: Sens. Kohl, Durbin, Feingold, Clinton, and Schumer

against.name: Sen. Thad Cochran
against.role: Chair, Senate Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it to die in committee.

against.name: Meat and poultry processing trade associations
against.role: Industry groups representing slaughter and processing plants
against.what_they_did: Opposed legislation that would write pathogen limits into statute after courts had struck down the Agriculture Department's enforcement of its Salmonella performance standard.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and nine of the ten cosponsors were Democrats; the one Republican was Senator Specter of Pennsylvania, and the bill never got far enough for a roll-call vote that would show the parties' full positions.

industries.note: The bill would have required regular microbial testing, pathogen-reduction standards benchmarked to top performers, and removal of the 'inspected and passed' label from plants that fail — a direct cost and compliance burden on an industry whose interest in keeping standards off the statute book runs against the public's interest in safer food.
Mandatory, recurring microbial testing at every inspected establishment would create steady demand for pathogen testing services.
